stem: A developer must process 10,000 documents overnight to produce a non-urgent analytics report. Cost is the primary concern, and results are not needed until the following morning. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Send every request synchronously through the Messages API in parallel to finish as quickly as possible.
options.explanation: Sending requests synchronously in parallel does not reduce per-token cost, and speed is not the requirement here.

options.text: Use the Message Batches API, which processes large asynchronous workloads within a 24-hour window at reduced cost.
options.explanation: Correct. The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads at lower cost, which matches an overnight, non-urgent job.

options.text: Lower max_tokens on synchronous calls to minimize cost.
options.explanation: Lowering max_tokens risks truncated output and does not address the batch-versus-realtime tradeoff.

options.text: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of output quality.
options.explanation: Blindly downsizing the model sacrifices quality and does not address the batch-versus-realtime tradeoff.

stem: A fan app has a chat assistant that answers questions about last night's game. Users say that after a few messages it 'forgets' things they said earlier, such as their favorite team. The backend sends only the latest user message on each request to the Messages API. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: The model's context window is too small. Switch to a model with a larger context window.
options.explanation: Context size isn't the problem. A few chat turns are far below any current model's limit, and the earlier turns are never sent in the first place.

options.text: Set a higher temperature so the model reuses earlier information more readily.
options.explanation: Sampling settings have no effect on information that isn't in the request, and current models don't accept non-default sampling parameters.

options.text: Pass the previous response's ID in a session_id parameter so the API can look up and replay the earlier turns.
options.explanation: The Messages API has no session_id parameter that restores history. The client owns conversation state.

options.text: The API is stateless: store the conversation in the app and resend the prior turns with each request.
options.explanation: Correct. The Messages API keeps no server-side session. Each request must include the full conversation you want the model to see.

stem: After every week of games, a league analytics team submits about 2,000 recap requests (one per game per angle) through the Message Batches API. Their importer then writes the results into a spreadsheet by row number, in the order the requests were submitted. Several recaps end up attached to the wrong games. What should they change?

options.text: Give each request a unique custom_id (e.g. game ID + angle) and join the results on it.
options.explanation: Correct. Batch results can come back in any order. The custom_id is how each result is matched to its request.

options.text: Submit the requests in small batches one after another, waiting for each to finish so results keep their submission order.
options.explanation: That defeats the point of batching, and the API still guarantees no particular order for results.

options.text: Sort the results by the time each one finished before importing them.
options.explanation: Completion order is not submission order either. Only the custom_id reliably identifies a result.

options.text: Switch to synchronous Messages API calls, because batches can't be used for structured output.
options.explanation: Batches accept the same request parameters as the Messages API. The bug is in how results are matched, not in batching.

stem: A team builds a 'live game companion' that writes a long play-by-play analysis while the user watches. Users complain that nothing appears for 20–40 seconds, and some long requests fail with client timeouts. Which change best addresses both problems?

options.text: Use the Message Batches API so long requests run asynchronously.
options.explanation: Batches can take a long time to finish, so they don't suit an interactive feature that needs output within seconds.

options.text: Stream the response and render the text deltas as they arrive.
options.explanation: Correct. Streaming shows tokens progressively, which shortens perceived latency, and it avoids HTTP timeouts on long generations. The SDKs recommend it for large max_tokens.

options.text: Lower max_tokens so each response finishes sooner, and show a loading spinner while the full answer is generated.
options.explanation: This cuts the analysis short and only treats the symptom. Users still wait for the whole response before seeing anything.

options.text: Raise the client's retry count so timed-out requests get retried automatically.
options.explanation: Retrying a request that times out repeats the same timeout and multiplies cost, and users still see nothing in the meantime.

stem: A fantasy assistant defines two tools, get_player_stats and get_injury_status. For one lineup question, Claude returns a single assistant message containing three tool_use blocks. How should the application send the results back? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Put all three tool_result blocks in a single user message, each with the matching tool_use_id.
options.explanation: Correct. Parallel tool calls are answered together in one user message, matched by tool_use_id. Splitting them across several messages discourages future parallel calls.

options.text: Send three separate user messages, one tool_result per message, in the order the calls appeared.
options.explanation: Splitting the results breaks the parallel-call pattern and teaches the model to stop making parallel calls.

options.text: If one tool call fails, still return a tool_result for it, with is_error set to true and a helpful error message.
options.explanation: Correct. Every tool_use needs a matching tool_result. Marking the failure lets Claude recover, for example by retrying or asking the user.

options.text: Skip any tool call that failed, so the model isn't confused by error text.
options.explanation: A tool_use block left without a matching result makes the conversation invalid and hides the failure from the model.

options.text: Copy the tool results into the system prompt for the next request.
options.explanation: Tool results belong in tool_result blocks in the user turn. The system prompt is for stable, trusted instructions.

stem: A scouting assistant sends the same 30,000-token league rulebook with every request, and the team enabled prompt caching on it. Logs show cache_read_input_tokens is always 0. The system prompt starts with a line like 'Current time: 2026-10-20T17:42:13Z', followed by the rulebook. What is the best fix?

options.text: Increase the cache TTL to 1 hour.
options.explanation: A longer TTL doesn't help. Every request has a different prefix, so there is never a cache entry to read.

options.text: Add more cache_control breakpoints throughout the rulebook so that at least some of its sections are served from cache.
options.explanation: Every breakpoint is still preceded by the changing timestamp, so none of them would ever match.

options.text: Move the timestamp after the cached rulebook so the cached prefix is byte-identical on every request.
options.explanation: Correct. Caching works on an exact prefix match. Any changing byte before the breakpoint invalidates everything after it, so stable content must come first.

options.text: Disable streaming, because streamed responses can't use the cache.
options.explanation: Streaming and prompt caching work fine together. The cause is the changing prefix.

stem: An app asks Claude for a JSON depth chart of a full 53-man roster. Sometimes JSON.parse fails because the output ends mid-object. In those failing responses, stop_reason is "max_tokens". What should the application do?

options.text: Wrap JSON.parse in a try/catch and automatically close any open brackets and braces so the partial output still parses.
options.explanation: Patching the JSON hides missing data. You would get a 'valid' depth chart with players silently left out.

options.text: Retry the identical request until a response parses.
options.explanation: The same request hits the same cap. Retrying wastes money without fixing anything.

options.text: Treat it as a safety refusal and send the request to a different model.
options.explanation: A refusal has its own stop_reason ("refusal"). max_tokens is a length limit, not a policy decision.

options.text: Check stop_reason first; treat max_tokens as truncation and raise max_tokens (streaming) or split the request.
options.explanation: Correct. max_tokens means generation hit the cap and the output is incomplete. Detect it explicitly and give the model enough room, or ask for less per request.

stem: A play-by-play summarizer calls the Messages API on game day, when traffic is high. Which errors should the client normally retry with exponential backoff, respecting any retry-after header? (Select TWO.)

options.text: 400 invalid_request_error
options.explanation: A malformed request fails the same way every time. Fix the request instead of retrying it.

options.text: 429 rate_limit_error
options.explanation: Correct. Rate limits are temporary. Back off, honoring retry-after when it is present, then retry.

options.text: 401 authentication_error
options.explanation: A bad or missing API key won't fix itself. Retrying only adds noise and can trigger alerts.

options.text: 529 overloaded_error
options.explanation: Correct. Overload is a temporary, service-side condition, and retrying with backoff is the recommended response.

options.text: 413 request_too_large
options.explanation: The payload stays too large on every retry. Shrink the request or use a different input method instead.

stem: Each week, a team's medical staff publishes its injury report as a multi-page PDF. An assistant must answer dozens of different questions about the same report during the week, across many separate requests. Which approach is most efficient?

options.text: Upload the PDF once with the Files API, then reference it by file_id in a document content block in each request.
options.explanation: Correct. The Files API is designed for assets that are reused across requests. You upload once and reference the file by ID instead of re-sending base64 data every time.

options.text: Convert every PDF page to a screenshot and send all of the page images along with each new question users ask.
options.explanation: This re-uploads the whole report with every request and discards the text layer that PDF support can use.

options.text: Paste the raw PDF bytes into the system prompt as text.
options.explanation: Raw PDF bytes aren't readable text. PDFs must be sent as document blocks, either base64-encoded or by file_id.

options.text: Send the PDF only in the first request of the week; Claude remembers the document for all later requests that week.
options.explanation: The API keeps no state between requests. Every request has to include, or reference, the document.

stem: A sports-media company's security policy requires all AI inference to run inside its existing AWS account, under AWS billing and IAM controls. A developer proposes using Claude through Amazon Bedrock. What else should the developer do before committing to that design?

options.text: Nothing. Bedrock offers exactly the same features as the first-party API on the same day.
options.explanation: Feature availability differs across platforms. Some features are first-party only, or arrive on partners later.

options.text: Use the first-party Anthropic client and point base_url at the Bedrock endpoint.
options.explanation: Each platform has its own client class, with its own authentication. Overriding the URL on the first-party client is not the supported path.

options.text: Check the platform-availability docs for every feature the design needs, and use Bedrock's own client and model IDs.
options.explanation: Correct. Third-party platforms use their own clients, auth and model ID formats, and support some features differently. Check the requirements against each platform before committing.

options.text: Store a first-party Anthropic API key in AWS Secrets Manager so that the application technically runs everything inside AWS.
options.explanation: Inference would still run on Anthropic's first-party API, which breaks the policy's intent that inference and billing stay in AWS.

stem: A league runs two Claude workloads: (1) push alerts that explain a scoring play to fans within seconds of it happening, and (2) a nightly job that writes detailed scouting notes for every player who appeared that day. Which API choice fits each workload?

options.text: Use the Message Batches API for both, to minimize cost.
options.explanation: Batches are asynchronous and can take hours to finish, which doesn't work for alerts that must go out within seconds.

options.text: Use real-time Messages API calls for both workloads, because the Batches API doesn't support long outputs like scouting notes.
options.explanation: Batches accept the same parameters as real-time calls, including long outputs. Sending the nightly job in real time gives up the batch discount for no benefit.

options.text: Use the Message Batches API for the alerts and real-time calls for the nightly job.
options.explanation: This is backwards. The latency-critical workload ends up on the asynchronous API.

options.text: Real-time Messages API calls for the alerts; the Message Batches API for the nightly scouting notes.
options.explanation: Correct. Latency-sensitive work goes through the real-time API. High-volume work that can wait goes through batches, at reduced cost.

stem: A team turned on prompt caching for a large, stable system prompt holding the league's statistical glossary. They want to confirm, from their production logs, that caching is actually working. What should they monitor?

options.text: The usage fields: cache_creation_input_tokens on the first write, then non-zero cache_read_input_tokens.
options.explanation: Correct. The usage block reports cache writes and reads directly, so it is the authoritative signal that caching works.

options.text: Lower end-to-end latency on every request compared with the same requests sent before prompt caching was enabled.
options.explanation: Latency can vary for many reasons. It is indirect evidence at best, and a cache miss can still be fast.

options.text: Whether the response text is identical across requests.
options.explanation: Caching reuses processed input. It does not make output deterministic, so identical answers prove nothing about the cache.

options.text: A cache_hit: true flag in the HTTP response headers.
options.explanation: Cache usage is reported in the response's usage object, not in a header flag.

stem: A trade-evaluation agent runs with thinking enabled and uses tools such as get_contract and get_cap_space. After the developer added code that removes thinking blocks from earlier assistant turns 'to save tokens', the multi-step tool loop began behaving inconsistently, and some requests are rejected. What is the best guidance?

options.text: Keep stripping thinking blocks, but also reset the conversation after each tool call so every step starts with a clean context.
options.explanation: Resetting throws away the context the agent needs for a multi-step evaluation and doesn't fix the protocol violation.

options.text: Pass assistant content back unchanged, thinking blocks included; manage tokens with effort or context-management features.
options.explanation: Correct. Thinking blocks must be passed back unchanged during tool use so the model keeps its reasoning chain. Editing or removing them can cause errors or degraded behavior. Use the supported controls to manage cost.

options.text: Disable thinking for the whole agent, because thinking and tool use can't be combined in the same multi-step conversation.
options.explanation: Thinking and tool use are designed to work together. Turning thinking off removes reasoning the task benefits from, and some current models don't allow it at all.

options.text: Turn the thinking text into a normal text block before sending it back.
options.explanation: Rewriting thinking blocks into another block type is still an edit to the history, and it can feed reasoning summaries back as if they were user-visible text.

stem: A coaching app lets assistants photograph whiteboard play diagrams with their phones and ask Claude what each play is designed to do. The answers are good, but each request takes noticeably long because the photos are full-resolution 12-megapixel images. Which change best reduces the delay without hurting answer quality?

options.text: Convert each photo into a one-page PDF so it is processed as a document rather than as an image.
options.explanation: PDF pages are also processed visually and billed as input. Wrapping the photo in a PDF adds conversion work and doesn't shrink what has to be sent and processed.

options.text: Resize each photo in the app to roughly the model's maximum native resolution before sending it.
options.explanation: Correct. Images larger than the model's native limit are downscaled by the API anyway, so the extra pixels only add upload size and latency. Resizing first keeps the detail Claude actually uses and cuts the payload.

options.text: Turn on streaming so the image uploads in chunks while Claude begins to analyze it.
options.explanation: Streaming applies to the response, not the request. It shows output sooner but doesn't make a large image upload any smaller or faster.

options.text: Put the question text before the image so Claude can start drafting its answer sooner.
options.explanation: Block order doesn't change the payload size. The docs also recommend placing images before the text that asks about them, so this would work against best practice.

stem: A film-study assistant lets analysts discuss the same twelve game-film screenshots across conversations that run 30 turns or more. The screenshots are sent as base64 image blocks, and as conversations grow, requests become very large and slow. The analysts still need Claude to look at the screenshots in later turns. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Rely on prompt caching, which stops the image bytes from being transmitted again after the first turn.
options.explanation: Caching lowers the cost and processing time of a repeated prefix, but every request still carries the full content. It doesn't shrink a payload that resends twelve base64 images each turn.

options.text: Send the screenshots only in the first turn, because the API keeps them available for the rest of the conversation.
options.explanation: The Messages API is stateless. If later requests omit the images, Claude can no longer see them.

options.text: Merge the twelve screenshots into one large collage so only a single image block is resent each turn.
options.explanation: A collage larger than the model's native resolution is downscaled as one image, so each frame loses detail. The analysts need to see each screenshot clearly.

options.text: Upload each screenshot once with the Files API and reference it by its file_id in every turn.
options.explanation: Correct. A file_id reference keeps request payloads small no matter how many images accumulate in the history, while Claude still sees each image on every turn.

stem: A sports-media company standardizes on Google Cloud and wants to call Claude through Vertex AI so usage appears on its existing cloud bill. The current first-party design sends highlight images as URL sources and runs a nightly job of 5,000 recap requests through the Message Batches API. What should the team address before committing to the move?

options.text: Some features the design relies on, including URL image sources and the Message Batches API, aren't offered there, so they must check availability per feature and plan alternatives.
options.explanation: Correct. Feature availability differs by platform. On Google Cloud, images must be sent as base64 and the Message Batches API isn't available, so both parts of the design need a replacement before the move.

options.text: Vertex AI requests still need an Anthropic API key alongside Google credentials, so the team must provision and rotate keys on both sides.
options.explanation: Claude on Vertex AI authenticates with Google Cloud credentials. No Anthropic API key is involved.

options.text: Nothing else changes, because they only need to point the first-party client's base_url at the Vertex AI endpoint and keep every request as it is.
options.explanation: Each cloud platform has its own client class and auth. Changing base_url on the first-party client isn't the supported path, and it wouldn't make missing features appear.

options.text: Prices, model availability and retirement dates on Vertex AI always match the first-party schedule, so the cost model can stay unchanged.
options.explanation: Partner-operated platforms set their own pricing and lifecycle dates, and model availability varies by region. The cost model has to be rebuilt from the platform's own terms.

stem: A league operations assistant answers staff questions about two sources: a 300-page collective bargaining agreement that changes once a year and is used in thousands of requests, and a player-availability service that updates every few minutes on game days. Which two data access patterns best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Put a snapshot of the player-availability feed into the system prompt each time the service is deployed.
options.explanation: A deploy-time snapshot goes stale within minutes on game day, so answers about availability would be wrong.

options.text: Upload the agreement once through the Files API and reference its file_id in each request that needs it.
options.explanation: Correct. A large, stable document used across many requests is the Files API's use case: upload once and reference it by ID instead of resending the bytes. Its content is billed as input tokens when used, and caching can reduce that further.

options.text: Let the staff app send any file_id it chooses, so each user can attach their own league documents.
options.explanation: Files are scoped to the workspace, not to a user. Accepting file IDs from clients would let one user read files that someone else uploaded. Keep file IDs server-side.

options.text: Send the agreement in the first request of each user session, since the API keeps it available until the session ends.
options.explanation: The Messages API keeps no session state. Content left out of a request is simply not visible to Claude in that request.

options.text: Give Claude a tool that queries the availability service whenever a question depends on current status.
options.explanation: Correct. Data that changes often, or of which only a slice is needed, is best fetched on demand through a tool, so every answer uses current values.

stem: A cap-analysis endpoint runs on a current Claude model with adaptive thinking at high effort. Because answers are usually two short paragraphs, the developer set max_tokens to 1,500. On hard questions, some responses now end with stop_reason "max_tokens" and contain little or no answer text. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add a thinking budget_tokens value of 1,024 so the reasoning gets its own allowance separate from max_tokens.
options.explanation: Fixed thinking budgets are rejected on current models, and even on older models budget_tokens had to fit inside max_tokens rather than adding to it.

options.text: Set the thinking display option to omitted so the hidden reasoning no longer counts toward the limit.
options.explanation: Display only controls whether thinking text is returned. The model still thinks, and those tokens are still billed and counted against max_tokens.

options.text: Raise max_tokens to leave room for thinking plus the answer, or lower effort if this route doesn't need deep reasoning.
options.explanation: Correct. Thinking tokens are output tokens and count against max_tokens, so hard questions used up the cap before the answer. Give the response more room (streaming if it gets large) or reduce effort for this route.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 so the model reasons more directly and reaches its answer in fewer tokens.
options.explanation: Temperature doesn't control thinking length, and non-default sampling values are rejected on current models.

stem: A fantasy-football advice chat runs on a current Claude model with adaptive thinking. Users see a long pause before the answer starts, and the developer notices the streamed thinking blocks contain empty text. Product wants the UI to show readable reasoning progress while Claude works. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Switch to a fixed budget_tokens configuration, which returns the model's full raw chain of thought.
options.explanation: Fixed budgets are rejected on current models, and no thinking mode returns the raw chain of thought.

options.text: Decode the signature field on each thinking block to recover the reasoning text that was hidden.
options.explanation: The signature is an opaque verification value used when blocks are passed back. It doesn't contain readable reasoning.

options.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt to write its reasoning in the visible answer inside thinking tags.
options.explanation: This duplicates reasoning into billed answer text, mixes it into what users read, and isn't the supported mechanism for showing thinking.

options.text: Request summarized thinking display so the streamed thinking blocks carry a readable summary.
options.explanation: Correct. On current models the default display omits thinking text, which is why the blocks are empty. Opting in to the summarized display streams a readable summary of the reasoning.

stem: A team-photo app wants to tag sideline photos with the players who appear in them, and the developer plans to ask Claude to name each player from their face. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Have Claude read visible jersey numbers and team colors, then map them to the roster in application code.
options.explanation: Correct. Claude doesn't identify people by name from their faces and declines such requests. Reading visible cues such as numbers and colors, then joining to roster data you control, gives a reliable tagging path.

options.text: Send higher-resolution face crops so Claude can match each face to the players it learned about in training.
options.explanation: Resolution isn't the obstacle. Naming people from facial features is a documented limitation, and Claude declines it.

options.text: Include the team's headshot gallery in the prompt so Claude can match faces against it.
options.explanation: Supplying reference photos doesn't change the limitation. Claude still won't identify people by their faces.

options.text: Add a system prompt stating that the league has consent from every player, so face identification is allowed.
options.explanation: A consent statement in the prompt doesn't lift the limitation, and the requests would still be declined.

stem: A multi-club scouting app uploads each club's documents through the Files API with one company API key. To let analysts ask about a document, the front end sends its `file_id` to the back end, which passes it straight into the Messages request. A security review flags this. Which design best fits?

options.text: Keep the design but make `file_id` values longer and harder to guess
options.explanation: Obscure IDs can still leak or be shared, and the back end would still accept them from anyone.

options.text: Upload every document again on each request instead of using the Files API
options.explanation: This removes the benefit of uploading once and doesn't fix the missing access check.

options.text: Map files to owners server-side and never accept a `file_id` from users
options.explanation: Correct. Files are scoped to the workspace, not to an end user, so any valid ID works for any caller. The app must decide which files a user may reference.

options.text: Ask Claude in the system prompt to refuse documents that belong to another club
options.explanation: Claude can't see who owns a file, and a prompt is not access control. The check belongs in the back end.

stem: During a busy weekend, a few hundred requests in a 10,000-request Message Batches job come back with result type `expired`. Finance asks whether they were billed, and the analytics team needs every result. Which response best fits?

options.text: They were billed at the batch rate; switch the whole job to real-time calls to avoid paying for expired requests
options.explanation: Expired requests aren't billed, and moving everything to real time would double the price of the work that did succeed.

options.text: They weren't billed; resubmit just the expired requests, identified by `custom_id`, in a new batch
options.explanation: Correct. Requests not processed within 24 hours expire without charge. Resubmitting only those, keyed by `custom_id`, completes the dataset at batch price.

options.text: They weren't billed, but expired requests can't be retried, so the missing results are lost
options.explanation: Nothing stops you sending the same requests again. Expiry just means they weren't processed in time.

options.text: They were billed in full; ask support to refund them and wait for the batch to finish them later
options.explanation: There is nothing to refund, and an expired request is never processed by that batch.

stem: A nightly job writes a scouting note for each of 1,500 players. A developer wants each request in a Message Batches job to call `get_stats` and `get_injuries` tools, read the results and then write the note. Which design best fits the Batch API?

options.text: Add both tools to every batch request and let each request run its own tool loop to completion
options.explanation: Batch requests are single-shot. A response that asks for a tool can't receive the result inside the batch.

options.text: Stream each batch request so the tool calls are handled as they arrive
options.explanation: Streaming isn't available inside a batch, and it wouldn't add a tool loop anyway.

options.text: Use the real-time API for all 1,500 notes, since batches can't use any data
options.explanation: Batches can use any data you include in the request. Giving up the batch discount isn't necessary.

options.text: Fetch each player's stats and injuries first, then put that data in the batch request
options.explanation: Correct. Gathering the data in code before submission turns each note into a single-shot request, which is what the Batch API processes at half price.

stem: A season-review generator uses a very large `max_tokens`, so the SDK requires streaming. The team doesn't show partial text to anyone; it only needs the finished message. Its hand-written code joins text deltas and occasionally breaks on `ping` events and multiple content blocks. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Turn streaming off and keep the large `max_tokens` with a longer client timeout
options.explanation: Long non-streaming requests are what the SDK's streaming requirement is meant to prevent, and they risk HTTP timeouts.

options.text: Keep streaming, but collect the result with the SDK's final-message helper
options.explanation: Correct. The SDK's helper (`get_final_message()` in Python, `finalMessage()` in TypeScript) handles every event type and assembles the complete message, so the team keeps streaming's timeout protection without parsing events by hand.

options.text: Filter out `ping` events and keep only the first content block in the custom assembler
options.explanation: Dropping later blocks loses content, and this keeps the team maintaining event handling the SDK already provides.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` so the SDK no longer requires streaming
options.explanation: The reviews would be truncated. The output length is a requirement, not something to cut for convenience.

stem: A week-long rules-research agent keeps appending tool results to one conversation. Responses start ending early with `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"`. A developer proposes raising `max_tokens` to fix it. Which response best fits?

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` as proposed, since the response was cut off before Claude finished
options.explanation: `max_tokens` caps the output only. The limit being hit here is the total context, so a bigger cap can't help.

options.text: Retry the same request, because the stop is a transient server-side condition
options.explanation: The context will be just as full on the retry. The condition comes from the conversation's size.

options.text: Shrink the context: clear stale tool results, compact, or use sub-agents
options.explanation: Correct. This stop means generation reached the context window limit, so the fix is to send less context, not to allow more output.

options.text: Treat the partial output as complete, since the agent had already gathered enough material
options.explanation: The answer was cut off, so using it as complete silently ships unfinished work.

stem: A film-study request sends a long question about route concepts first, then six screenshots of the formation as image blocks at the end of the user message. Answers are good but often generic. Which change to the request most directly follows the recommended pattern?

options.text: Convert the screenshots into a text description and drop the images
options.explanation: Describing the images loses detail Claude could have read from them directly.

options.text: Send each screenshot in a separate request and combine the answers
options.explanation: Splitting the images stops Claude comparing them, which the question needs.

options.text: Place the image blocks before the question in the user message
options.explanation: Correct. Putting images first and the question after them is the recommended order for image-based prompts.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` so Claude can describe every image in more detail
options.explanation: A larger cap allows longer answers but doesn't change how the request is structured.

stem: A team's pipeline runs OCR on weekly injury-trend PDFs and sends Claude only the extracted text. Questions about the charts in those PDFs, such as "Which position group's injuries rose fastest?", get poor answers. Which change best fits?

options.text: Improve the OCR settings so the chart labels are extracted more accurately
options.explanation: Better labels still lose the chart itself, which is what the question is about.

options.text: Ask Claude to infer the chart trends from the surrounding text
options.explanation: If the trends aren't written out in the text, Claude can only guess.

options.text: Switch to the Message Batches API so each PDF gets more processing time
options.explanation: Batch processing changes cost and timing, not what content Claude receives.

options.text: Send the PDFs as `document` blocks so Claude reads text and visuals
options.explanation: Correct. With PDF support, Claude sees each page's text and its charts and images, so chart questions can be answered from the source.

stem: A finance lead asks the team to turn on streaming for a nightly job that writes 3,000 player summaries nobody reads until morning, "to make it cheaper". Which response best fits?

options.text: Streaming doesn't lower cost; move the job to the Message Batches API
options.explanation: Correct. Streaming improves latency and avoids timeouts but is priced the same. For work nobody waits on, the Batch API cuts the price by half.

options.text: Turn on streaming, since streamed tokens are billed at a lower rate
options.explanation: Streamed and non-streamed tokens are priced the same.

options.text: Turn on streaming and lower `max_tokens` to save on output
options.explanation: A lower cap risks truncated summaries and retries, and streaming still saves nothing.

options.text: Keep the job as is, because no API option reduces the cost of overnight work
options.explanation: The Batch API exists precisely for asynchronous, non-urgent work at lower cost.

stem: A medical-staff assistant on a current Claude model runs with thinking and tools. To meet a privacy rule, the harness rewrites earlier user and assistant turns on every request to mask player names. Requests start failing or losing reasoning partway through tool loops. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Keep rewriting history but strip all thinking blocks so nothing depends on them
options.explanation: Stripping thinking blocks breaks tool loops on current models and discards the reasoning they carry.

options.text: Mask names before content enters the conversation; keep history append-only
options.explanation: Correct. On the newest models a thinking block stays valid only while everything before it is unchanged. Masking at the point of entry meets the privacy rule without editing history.

options.text: Turn off thinking for the whole feature so history edits no longer matter
options.explanation: Some current models can't disable thinking, and turning it off would lower quality on a feature that relies on it.

options.text: Retry each failed request until the edited history is accepted
options.explanation: The edit itself causes the failure. Retrying the same edited history fails the same way.

stem: A developer enables Anthropic's server-side web search tool for a trade-rumor assistant. They then write code that waits for `stop_reason: "tool_use"`, runs a web search through a third-party API, and sends back a `tool_result`, but the loop never sees a web search call. What is the misunderstanding?

options.text: Web search requires a forced `tool_choice` before Claude will call it
options.explanation: Forced tool choice isn't required, and it is rejected on some current models anyway.

options.text: Web search only works in the Message Batches API, not in real-time requests
options.explanation: Server tools work in ordinary Messages requests.

options.text: Server tools run on Anthropic's side and their results come back in the same response
options.explanation: Correct. Your code doesn't execute server tools. The search happens on Anthropic's infrastructure and its results arrive as content blocks in the response.

options.text: Web search needs a `tool_result` sent before the first request so Claude knows it works
options.explanation: There is nothing to send in advance. A `tool_result` answers a client tool call, which this isn't.

stem: A trade-rumor assistant enables the server-side web fetch tool. A user asks it to "fetch the latest article on the team's website about the trade" without giving a URL, and Claude says it can't fetch the page. What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: Web fetch can't access news sites, so the article has to be scraped by the application instead.
options.explanation: There is no blanket ban on news sites. Domain restrictions are something the developer configures.

options.text: The code execution tool must also be declared, because web fetch runs inside it.
options.explanation: On current models, dynamic filtering runs code execution internally. Declaring a separate code execution tool is unnecessary and can confuse the model.

options.text: Web fetch requires a beta header, and without it the tool is silently ignored.
options.explanation: Web fetch is a server tool declared in tools. The failure comes from the missing URL, not from a header.

options.text: Web fetch only retrieves URLs that already appear in the conversation. The user should supply the URL, or the app should also enable web search so that results provide URLs to fetch.
options.explanation: Correct. Web fetch is limited to URLs already present in the conversation, for example from the user or from earlier search results. Adding web search provides those URLs.

stem: A document Q&A endpoint sometimes receives uploads so large that requests fail after a long wait. The team wants to detect oversized requests before sending them and route those to a chunking path, using the same token counts the model will actually see. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Call the token counting endpoint with the same model, system prompt, messages and tools, and compare the result with the model's context limit.
options.explanation: Correct. count_tokens uses the model's own tokenizer and accounts for the system prompt, tools and attachments, so its result matches what the request will consume.

options.text: Count tokens locally with an open-source tokenizer from another model provider, which is faster than an API call.
options.explanation: Other providers' tokenizers count differently and tend to undercount Claude tokens, so oversized requests would slip through.

options.text: Estimate tokens as characters divided by four, and leave a 20% safety margin.
options.explanation: The ratio varies widely with language, code and formatting, and newer tokenizers produce more tokens for the same text. A heuristic can't match the real count.

options.text: Send every request and switch to chunking only when the API returns an error.
options.explanation: This spends the upload and wait time the team wants to avoid, and doesn't detect the problem in advance.

stem: A RAG assistant retrieves passages from the league's internal operations wiki through a custom search tool. Compliance wants each answer to carry citations that name the wiki page title and URL, the same way web search results are cited. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Put all retrieved passages in the system prompt and instruct Claude to name its sources in brackets.
options.explanation: Bracketed sources written as prose are self-reported and unverifiable, and the system prompt is the wrong place for retrieved data.

options.text: Enable the web search tool with allowed_domains set to the wiki's domain.
options.explanation: The wiki is internal, so the public web search tool can't reach it. The passages are already retrieved by the custom tool.

options.text: Use structured outputs with a sources array that Claude fills in with the page titles it used.
options.explanation: A schema field is still self-reported attribution. It isn't tied to the retrieved text.

options.text: Return the retrieved passages from the tool as search_result content blocks, each with source, title and content, with citations enabled.
options.explanation: Correct. Search result blocks let Claude cite your own content with source and title attribution, and each citation points back to the passage.

stem: A rules-desk tool sends three PDF rulebooks as document blocks and wants answers with citations. A developer is reviewing how citations work. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Citations can be combined with output_config.format to get JSON answers that include citation objects.
options.explanation: Citations are incompatible with structured outputs, and the combination returns a 400 error.

options.text: Citations must be enabled on all of the documents in a request or on none of them.
options.explanation: Correct. Enabling citations on only some of the documents isn't supported.

options.text: Citations require a beta header on the Messages API.
options.explanation: Citations are generally available and need no beta header.

options.text: The answer arrives as a single text block with a list of citations appended at the end.
options.explanation: The response is split into several text blocks, and the blocks that make claims carry their own citations arrays.

options.text: For PDF documents, each citation reports the cited text with a page_location giving start and end page numbers.
options.explanation: Correct. Citations from PDFs use page locations. Plain-text documents use character locations instead.

stem: A play-suggestion feature asks Claude to list candidate plays inside <plays>...</plays> tags. To save output tokens, the developer adds stop_sequences: ["</plays>"]. Generation now stops at the right place, but the downstream parser fails because the closing tag is missing. What is happening, and what is the fix?

options.text: The matched stop sequence isn't included in the returned text. When stop_reason is "stop_sequence", the code should append the tag (the stop_sequence field says which sequence matched) or parse without requiring it.
options.explanation: Correct. The API stops before emitting the stop sequence and reports which one matched. Parsing has to account for that.

options.text: Stop sequences are only supported with streaming, so non-streaming responses drop the final characters.
options.explanation: Stop sequences work with both streaming and non-streaming requests.

options.text: The model ignores stop sequences when the text contains XML, so the response ended for another reason.
options.explanation: Stop sequences match on generated text regardless of its format. Generation stopped because the sequence matched.

options.text: Stop sequences are applied only after max_tokens is reached, so the tag is cut off by truncation.
options.explanation: Stop sequences end generation as soon as they match, independently of max_tokens.

stem: An analytics team wants Claude to compute season aggregates, such as yards per play by down and distance, from a 40 MB play-by-play CSV. Pasting the CSV into the prompt exceeds the context window, and asking Claude to do arithmetic over thousands of rows in its head is unreliable. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Convert the CSV to JSON so that it uses fewer tokens and fits in one request.
options.explanation: JSON is usually more verbose than CSV, and the arithmetic problem would remain.

options.text: Upload the CSV with the Files API and make it available to the code execution tool, so Claude writes and runs analysis code in the sandbox and only the results enter context.
options.explanation: Correct. The file never has to fit in context. Code computes the aggregates exactly, and only the final numbers come back to Claude.

options.text: Send the CSV as an image of a spreadsheet so that the vision model can read it.
options.explanation: Images of tables lose precision and don't scale to a file of this size.

options.text: Split the CSV into chunks that fit the context window and ask Claude to sum each chunk, then add the partial sums by hand.
options.explanation: This still relies on the model's arithmetic over raw rows and adds a fragile manual merge step.

stem: An analyst tool sends a 60,000-token league rulebook with each request, cached with a default `cache_control` marker. Analysts ask a question about every 15 to 20 minutes, and the logs show a new cache write on almost every request. Which change best fits?

options.text: Set the rulebook's cache TTL to one hour, so the entry survives the gaps between questions
options.explanation: Correct. The default entry lives five minutes, so 15-to-20-minute gaps let it expire. The one-hour TTL costs more to write but keeps the entry alive between questions.

options.text: Move the rulebook after the analyst's question, so the stable content sits at the end of the prompt
options.explanation: Caching matches a prefix. Putting the varying question first would break the cache on every request.

options.text: Add a second cache breakpoint on the same rulebook block, which doubles the entry's lifetime
options.explanation: Extra breakpoints mark more cache positions. They don't extend how long an entry lives.

options.text: Send the questions through the Message Batches API, which keeps cached content for 24 hours
options.explanation: Batches are for asynchronous bulk work, not interactive questions, and they don't extend cache lifetime to 24 hours.

stem: A team charges internal departments for Claude usage based on the token counts in each streamed response. Long answers show almost no output tokens. The code records usage only from the `message_start` event. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Count the characters in every text delta and divide by four to estimate the output tokens
options.explanation: This is a rough estimate, not the billed count, and it ignores tokens that aren't visible text.

options.text: Turn streaming off, because streamed responses do not report output token usage at all
options.explanation: Streamed responses do report usage. The code is just reading it from the wrong event.

options.text: Read the cumulative usage in the final `message_delta` event, or take it from the SDK's final message
options.explanation: Correct. `message_start` arrives before any output is generated. The cumulative usage in the final `message_delta` reflects the whole response.

options.text: Send each finished answer to the token-counting endpoint and record the number it returns as output usage
options.explanation: Token counting estimates the size of a prompt. It doesn't report what this response was actually billed for.

stem: A film-review tool sends 30 sideline screenshots, each 3000×2000 pixels, as image blocks in one Messages API request. The request is rejected with an `invalid_request_error` that mentions many-image requests. Sending 15 of the same screenshots works. Which change best fits?

options.text: Upload the screenshots through the Files API instead, which lifts the per-image limits for the request
options.explanation: Referencing images by `file_id` keeps the payload small, but the per-image limits still apply to the request.

options.text: Resize each screenshot so neither side exceeds 2000 px, or send 20 images or fewer per request
options.explanation: Correct. Above 20 images in one request, a stricter per-image dimension limit applies. Smaller images or smaller groups both stay within it.

options.text: Combine the screenshots into one PDF, so that the request no longer contains any image blocks at all
options.explanation: Each PDF page is still processed as an image, and on some platforms document blocks count toward the same threshold, so this only moves the problem.

options.text: Retry the same request with exponential backoff until the API has enough capacity to accept it
options.explanation: This is an invalid request, not a capacity problem. The same request fails the same way on every retry.

stem: A team moves a play-tagging service to Claude Opus 5.5. The old code set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "record_tags"}` to guarantee a call with schema-valid input. Every request now fails with a 400 error about `tool_choice`. Which change best fits while keeping schema-valid tag data?

options.text: Keep the forced tool choice and repeat the tool's schema in the system prompt
options.explanation: The 400 comes from the forced `tool_choice` itself. Adding text to the prompt doesn't change that.

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}`, so Claude must call one of the tools
options.explanation: Forcing any tool is also rejected on this model, so the requests would still fail.

options.text: Ask for the tags as plain text and parse them out with a regular expression
options.explanation: This drops the schema guarantee the team relied on and adds fragile parsing.

options.text: Use `auto` with `strict: true` on the tool and an instruction to call it, or use structured outputs
options.explanation: Correct. Forced tool use isn't supported on this model. Strict tool schemas keep the input valid, and structured outputs fit when the call only existed to get JSON back.

stem: A nightly Message Batches job sends 3,000 requests that all share the same 20,000-token scouting glossary at the start of the system prompt. Prompt caching is on, but cache hits are low. Which TWO changes are most likely to raise the hit rate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Put identical `cache_control` markers on the glossary block in every request of the batch
options.explanation: Correct. Hits depend on matching prefixes and markers, so every request should mark the shared block the same way.

options.text: Use the one-hour cache TTL on the glossary, since batch processing can take longer than five minutes
options.explanation: Correct. Batch requests run asynchronously over a longer window, so a five-minute entry can expire between them.

options.text: Add a request with `max_tokens: 0` at the start of the batch to pre-warm the cache
options.explanation: Pre-warming with `max_tokens: 0` is not supported inside a batch.

options.text: Put each player's name at the very top of the system prompt, so requests are easy to trace
options.explanation: A value that differs per request at the start of the prompt breaks the shared prefix, so nothing after it can be read from cache.

options.text: Rely on a guaranteed hit for every request once the first request has written the cache
options.explanation: Batch requests run concurrently, so cache hits are best-effort. There is no guarantee to rely on.

stem: A fantasy chat assistant caches a long system prompt and its tool definitions. For a new "trade mode", a developer adds a `propose_trade` tool to the tools list only while the user is in that mode. Cache reads drop to zero on every mode switch. Which change best fits?

options.text: Send one fixed, sorted tool list on every request and signal the mode in the message content
options.explanation: Correct. Tools render first in the prompt, so any change to the list invalidates everything cached after it. A stable tool list keeps the prefix intact.

options.text: Move the cache breakpoint to the latest user message, so the cache covers the whole conversation
options.explanation: The breakpoint position doesn't matter when the tools at the start of the prefix keep changing.

options.text: Switch to a cheaper model while in trade mode, to offset the cost of the extra cache writes
options.explanation: Caches are scoped to a model, so switching models forces another full write instead of saving money.

options.text: Put a separate cache breakpoint on the `propose_trade` tool, so that it is cached on its own
options.explanation: Adding or removing a tool still changes the prefix that all later cache entries depend on.

stem: An app moved to Claude Sonnet 5.5. It used to end each request with a partial assistant turn containing `{` so that Claude would reply in JSON. Those requests now return a 400 error. Which change best fits?

options.text: Prefill a longer string, such as the first key of the expected object, in the assistant turn
options.explanation: Any assistant prefill is rejected on this model, however long it is.

options.text: Remove the prefill and use structured outputs with a JSON schema in `output_config.format`
options.explanation: Correct. Prefilling isn't supported on current models. Structured outputs guarantee JSON that matches the schema.

options.text: Send the opening brace as a second user message instead of in an assistant turn
options.explanation: This only adds an odd user message. It doesn't constrain the output format.

options.text: Pin an older version of the SDK, so the prefill is sent the way it used to be
options.explanation: The API rejects the request, not the SDK, so an older SDK sends the same failing request.
